svg.title: The send-gate: three deterministic checks after human approval
svg.desc: A hand-drawn flow of four stages: the agent drafts, a human approves, edits, or rejects, a deterministic send-gate runs three checks, and only then does Gmail send, with an audit row. A caption notes a human can approve a draft that still breaks a rule, which is why the gate runs after them rather than instead of them. Three cards give the checks, each with its condition in code: a URL allow-list rejecting any link that did not appear in the thread or a known set, closing the exfiltration channel by hand; a money check refusing any monetary term the thread never contained, because a commitment is not a tone decision; and a business-hours check rejecting proposed times outside them, catching the case where the model guessed instead of calling its calendar tool. Captions state that the model proposes and the application enforces, and that a blocked draft goes back to the human with its reason, which then becomes a fixture.
svg.text: The human approves, and the deterministic guard still runs. Neither replaces the other.
A human can approve a draft that still breaks a rule. That is exactly why the gate runs after them, not instead of them.
No URL that did not appear in the thread
or in a known set. This is the
The draft cannot introduce a monetary term
the thread never contained. A commitment
No proposed time outside business hours.
The model has no calendar; it has a tool,
and this catches when it guessed instead.
The model proposed; the application enforces. Three concrete checks, and the agent can produce drafts that fail any of them.
The system does the right thing without depending on the prompt to forbid it, which is the whole of Post 23's first defence.
A blocked draft is not a failure to hide. It goes back to the human with the reason, and the reason becomes a fixture.
